morning.title: Tejas Mk2 IRST Completes Developmental Trials, Certification
morning.text:
The Infra-Red Search and Tracking (IRST) system to be fitted on the Tejas Mk2 has completed development and qualification. Further testing of the system will occur on the Tejas Mk2.
Instead of a completely new IRST being developed specifically for the Tejas Mk2 fighter aircraft, technology developed for the Su-30MKI program will be used. This development has been led by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL).
This passive Electro-Optical system detects aircraft in the far-infrared part of the spectrum, and can be used to detect and monitor aerial targets in situations where it is desirable to avoid radar emissions.
Although development and qualification has been completed, further platform specific testing needs to be performed on the Tejas Mk2 in order to assess the performance of this system, ensure compatibility with the aircraft, and understand how it will interact with the onboard avionic and mission equipment.
Su-30MKI
The indigenous IRST was developed to replace the Russian derived Optical Locator Sensor (OLS) currently installed on the Su-30MKI. A more capable system was required with greater performance, serviceability and reliability.
A collaboration contract was signed between HAL and BEL on 26th April 2022 to develop and manufacture a Long Range Dual Band Infrared Search and Tracking system together as a Make-II project under the Defence Acquisition Procedure.
This system contains Television (day), Infrared, and Laser sensors. It can be used for tracking and locating aerial and ground targets. As a passive system, it can be valuable to the pilot in various situations.
The project is led by HAL. BEL are collaborating in development and manufacturing. Initially, it was aimed to upgrade the Su-30MKI fleet with an indigenously developed optical location system. Testing on the Tejas Mk2
By using the same system on the Tejas Mk2, the scope of this project is increased. Within the indigenous fighter development program, a long range dual band IRST system can be utilised without starting a separate development project.
Despite development and qualification being complete, testing within the Tejas Mk2 aircraft must still be performed to prove the performance of the system. This testing must prove that the system is installed correctly on the Tejas Mk2, and that it has the correct field of view, electrical/data interfaces, correct cooling, software integration, and compatibility with the mission computer.
It was previously requested by the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) that support from industry would be required to integrate, test and qualify the IRST, Software Defined Radio (SDR), and Combined Interrogator/Transponder (CIT) systems on the Tejas Mk2. This shows that the integration of these systems onto the Tejas Mk2 is a separate development process to qualifying the systems themselves.
Using this Su-30MKI developed IRST system on the Tejas Mk2 means that there is a common indigenous system base within different fighter aircraft types within India. It provides an opportunity to standardise maintenance, support infrastructure, and future upgrade processes between different aircraft. However, final designs may vary depending on the particular installation requirements for each aircraft.
Whilst this system will be used to replace the OLS-30 in the Su-30MKI, it will act as a new passive detection/ tracking system, as part of the state-of-the-art sensor package in the Tejas Mk2.

morning.title: ePlane Selects LYNX MOSA.ic to Run Safety-Critical Software on e200X eVTOL
morning.text:
Lynx, a leader in safe and secure software platforms for mission-critical edge systems, today announced at eVTOL Show USA that The ePlane Company has selected LYNX MOSA.ic as the mixed-criticality software platform for mission computing on its e200X eVTOL. The e200X is a 3-seat (pilot + 2 passengers) lift and cruise eVTOL with a modular airframe designed for air ambulance, urban cargo, and passenger service. Each variant carries a different payload, sensor set, and software stack, while flight control stays deterministic and certifiable in every configuration.
LYNX MOSA.ic partitions the e200X’s onboard compute so flight-critical software, such as the vehicle and energy management systems, runs in ARINC 653 partitions, isolated from lower-criticality mission functions that handle sensor data processing and situational awareness inference. Heavy AI processing runs on a separate platform, and the mission system supplies the controlled interfaces between that platform and the rest of the aircraft, ensuring clear cybersecurity and safety isolation.
“A multi-role aircraft asks more of its computers than a single-mission design, because the mission software keeps changing while flight control cannot,” said Tim Reed, Chief Executive Officer of Lynx. “LYNX MOSA.ic lets ePlane keep flight-critical software isolated and certifiable while its pilot assist software evolves with each role.”
LYNX MOSA.ic is a mixed-criticality operating environment built around a separation kernel-based type 1 hypervisor. It gives each software subject its own space and time partition, so applications at different levels of criticality can share one platform, and it is certifiable to DO-178C DAL A.
“Urban air mobility is as much a computational challenge as it is an aerodynamic one. Operating high-density routes safely across emergency response, logistics, and passenger transit requires mission computing that is both certifiably safe and functionally modular. LYNX MOSA.ic gives us the deterministic partitioning required to isolate safety-critical systems while our engineers build cutting-edge aircraft functionalities on familiar tools. It is a foundational technology for delivering scalable, multi-role electric aviation,” said Prof. Satya Chakravarthy, Founder and Technical Lead, The ePlane Company.
Lynx will take the stage at eVTOL Show USA on Tuesday, November 17, at 11:35 a.m. in the Gateway Ballroom at the Santa Clara Convention Center to present “Building the Certifiable Software Behind Electric Flight.” Attendees are also invited to connect with the Lynx team at Booth #33.

morning.title: IAF Identifies Astra Mk-II as Main BVRAAM for 114 Rafale F4+ Fighters
morning.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)’s Armament Research & Development Establishment (ARDE) developed the Astra MkII Er with a range up to 200-220 km, which has been selected by the Indian Air Force (IAF) to be the main Beyond Visual Range Air-to-Air Missile (BVRAAM) for the 114 Rafale Fleet that will be based on the F4 Plus configuration that will be a customised variant of the Rafale Variant that will carry many of the customised features that are on the current Rafale 3FR fleet plus more advanced features that have been identified for the jets that are to be made in the country.
IDRW has learned from its sources that IAF is keen to make locally developed Astra MkII as the main BVRAAM on the whole fleet, not depending on the MBDA-supplied Meteor missiles. Dassault already has been convened about IAF’s requirements and has been agreed upon so that the missile can be integrated directly with the mission computer and the Thales RBE2 AESA radar and SPECTRA electronic warfare suite for enhanced situational awareness and survivability.
ARDE has already commenced trials of the Astra MkII, which has demonstrated a range up to 220 km under computer-aided simulation. After getting a major propulsion chemistry upgrade, trials are ongoing to demonstrate the take-down of targets at such ranges in the next phase. MKII, which uses a dual-pulse rocket motor initially, was designed to have a range of 160 km that was bumped up from the original plan of 145 km over the course of the last decade.
The prolonged developmental cycle of the Astra MkI that has lasted over 2 decades now has allowed ARDE to come up with better systems and propulsions that have allowed the weapon to increase its range over the period of time to keep up with demands of the modern combat, where ranges up to 145-200 in air-to-air missiles are becoming a norm now.
ARDE, from the initial range of 80, later demonstrated an MKI with a range up to 110 km, and now it has further bumped its range to 160 km, which is now entering the MKII range, but now the MKII range also has been bumped up towards 200-plus range. Now that could make it an ideal weapon of choice of the IAF to make it a standard type across the fleet.
IAF already has plans to procure up to 700 units of MkII BVRAAMS in the coming months, and the missile has already been offered to private sector companies as a full ToT to scale up the production speed and also to create two production lines in the country so that demands from IAF and also from prospective export customers can also be met.
IDRW has been told that in coming months Astra MkII production partners from the private sector might be announced soon, and two production lines will see complete integration of the missile instead of just assembly that will allow each production line to initially manufacture 100 units per year that can be further scaled up to 200 units per production line each year once the orders flow in for all types.
IAF plans to incorporate Astra MkII not only for the 114 Rafale F4+ fleet but also for the 36 Rafale 3FR fleet that will be upgraded to the F4+ fleet. Also, it will be the main weapon on the Mig-29 UPG, Su-30 MKI, and Tejas Mk1A and MkII. That will mean the IAF will be requiring around 1500-3000 units of this missile alone in the next 10-15 years for its own requirements as more and more fighter types are cleared for operational usage of the weapon.

morning.title: The Jet That Always Shadows Air Force One When The President Travels Abroad
morning.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent visit to China has drawn particular attention from online flight trackers. This is in no small part due to the fact that all three of the U.S. Air Force’s current Boeing 747-based Air Force One aircraft – the two older VC-25As and the new ex-Qatari VC-25B “Bridge” jet – have supported the trip. Another militarized 747, an E-4B Nightwatch, commonly referred to as a ‘doomsday plane,’ was also spotted shadowing the group to and from Asia.

While this drew a lot of attention online, including blog posts from defense-focused sites, the reality is this is absolutely standard practice. The E-4B is just another part, albeit a very unique and shy one, of the massive aerial logistics ballet that occurs whenever the President leaves the country.

The Air Force currently has four E-4Bs, also known as National Airborne Operations Centers (NAOC), all based at Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Based on the 747-200 model, three of these planes first entered service in the 1970s as E-4A Advanced Airborne Command Posts (AACP). Those aircraft were subsequently brought up to the E-4B NAOC standard in the 1980s, and were eventually joined by a fourth example converted straight to that configuration. The jets have been continuously upgraded over the years. In addition to supporting presidential travel, the Nightwatch aircraft also regularly transport the Secretary of Defense (now also referred to as the Secretary of War) and their staff during overseas trips, among other roles.

The VC-25s carrying Trump and the rest of his entourage left Andrews Air Force Base just outside Washington, D.C., on November 16. An E-4B was tracked heading out from Offutt at around the same time.

Trump headed first for a brief visit to the Philippines before traveling on to China. Plane spotters had a rare opportunity to see all three VC-25s parked together at Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila.

The Nightwatch jet headed separately to Kadena Air Base on the Japanese island of Okinawa.

All three VC-25s left China carrying Trump and the rest of the U.S. delegation earlier today. As the trio began to pass over Japan’s home islands, the E-4B took off from Kadena to follow them.

As mentioned at the start, the E-4B shadowing the VC-25s and being forward-deployed in Kadena during Trump’s visit to the Philippines and then China is no surprise. This is standard operating procedure for when the President of the United States travels abroad. Flight trackers notably caught a similar procession of aircraft during Trump’s trip to China back in May.

While the E-4Bs are nowhere near as luxurious as the VC-25As or the new VC-25B, they are just as capable of serving as airborne command posts, if not more so in many respects. They are unofficially referred to as ‘doomsday planes’ because they are specifically configured to provide the president and other senior military officials with a flying headquarters they can use for any and all duties, including directing nuclear strikes during the most serious crises. They are hardened against electromagnetic pulses caused by nuclear detonations and have the ability to stay airborne for days. Their very existence, at least one being on alert at all times to support the National Command Authority, is a critical component that underpins America’s nuclear deterrent. Even if an adversary destroys much of the country, an E-4 can remain airborne to order the counter-attack.

With all this in mind, the E-4B fleet is key to so-called continuity of government plans, which are in place to make sure key elements of the federal government remain functional following an attack or a similarly serious contingency. As a prime example, President George W. Bush rode on one of the VC-25A Air Force One aircraft in the immediate wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, but there were discussions about transferring him to a Nightwatch jet. Bush ultimately decided against making the change, but an E-4B was still scrambled and orbited over Washington, D.C., for a time. This is hardly the only time a president has made use of an E-4B, or one of its predecessors, as well as command ships, as TWZ has examined in the past.

Within this broader context, E-4Bs have been a key feature of overseas presidential travel for decades now, although they are the least visible of the presidential aerial armada. This massive airlift and logistics effort includes bringing in multiple examples of the presidential motorcade, Marine One helicopters, and various force protection assets. This involves many sorties by C-17 and C-5 cargo aircraft that cover many thousands of miles each. The videos below from Trump’s visit this week to the Philippines give a sense of just one portion of these options, albeit the most visible one, the vertical airlift component.

Beyond its strategic command and control mission, having an E-4B positioned in the region the president is visiting during overseas trips offers a critical option for refuge and escape, as well as an additional backup aircraft to Air Force One, should any emergencies arise. The exact parameters for where the Nightwatch aircraft go are unknown, but would be based on what suitable airports are available and what potential threats and contingencies could arise. They are never seen at the same locations as Air Force One and are always separated by a distance of dozens of miles, at least, in friendly countries — close enough to be accessed by Marine One in an emergency — or generally in a region for more sensitive locales where such close proximity basing isn’t an option.

E-4Bs do not need to be airborne to act as command and control platforms and secure communications relay nodes, either. This further feeds into their continuity of government role. These are capabilities that can also be made available, if required, to assist the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) during major natural disasters or to help serve as command posts and communications nodes in other emergencies.

The changing character of the Air Force One fleet could put new emphasis on the E-4Bs, as well as the replacement E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center (SAOC) jets the Air Force is now in the process of acquiring.

Trump’s trip back from China has notably underscored a significant difference between the VC-25As and the new VC-25B Bridge aircraft, which is that the latter lacks aerial refueling capability. Two fully-outfitted VC-25Bs that Boeing is still in the process of converting for the Air Force will also not be capable of refueling in flight. The E-4Bs can refuel in flight, and the E-4Cs will be able to do so, as well.

TWZ has previously explored the Air Force’s decision to axe the aerial refueling requirement for the VC-25B in detail. The ostensible logic is that the VC-25Bs are based on newer 747-8i aircraft with more capable and fuel-efficient engines than the aging 747-200-based VC-25As. The new aircraft are, as a result, capable of longer unrefueled flights, though maximum range requirements were also watered down.

At the same time, in-flight refueling allows the VC-25As (as well as the E-4Bs) to remain aloft for days at a time. This, in turn, could be critical in a major crisis where access to secure airfields might be limited, if not completely unavailable, for a prolonged period of time.

The VC-25B Bridge jet has prompted a whole new array of operational security questions, which TWZ was calling attention to even before the decision was formally made to outfit it for presidential use. The circumstances of Trump’s return from the NATO summit in Turkey in July had prompted a further flurry of reports about whether the modified, Qatari-gifted jet lacked sufficient defensive features and other capabilities in line with the existing VC-25As. The President had flown to Turkey on the Bridge jet, but was reportedly covertly moved between other aircraft on the way back. This was said to have been done as a security precaution amid then-escalating fighting with Iran.

President Trump subsequently downplayed the series of events, but said that the Bridge aircraft would be sent to have its capabilities “maxed out.” The White House confirmed that the jet would receive “additional upgrades and enhancements,” but did not elaborate. It is unclear how the aircraft’s configuration has changed in the ensuing months.

It is worth noting here that the upgrades in question would have to be limited to defensive systems. The Bridge aircraft could also have entered service without certain communications and networking capabilities found on the VC-25As. Another way to mitigate any such limitations could be to have a VC-25A or an E-4B operating closely enough to establish a line-of-sight data connection relatively quickly so it can leverage the better-equipped aircraft’s communications systems if needed.

As an aside, Trump arrived in China aboard the Bridge aircraft and was seen boarding it to head back to the United States. Reporters onboard had their phones taken away during the return flight for still unexplained security reasons. Fox News has reported that the president is aiming to set a record for the longest continuous flight for an Air Force One aircraft. At the time of writing, its unclear whether the president has touched back down anywhere publicly since leaving Shenzhen.

Where the E-4B is now is also unclear, but it was last tracked continuing along a path shadowing behind Air Force One, where one would expect to see it.

Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else
morning.text:
If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.

VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. VMSA-2026-0009 also details four more CVEs, some of them high-severity.

VMware’s second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618).

A KVM curiosity

Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours.

This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host.

It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5.

Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.

Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.

The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

morning.title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way
morning.text:
The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.

"Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them."

Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime.

"At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption."

Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering.

Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained.

Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network.

"Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life."

At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play.

Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content."

Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements.

"I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device."

If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success.

But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky.

Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose.

"On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app.

"And so the way that we're marketing and growing right now is [by offering] end-to-end encrypted messages for Bluesky users. You log in with your handle into our app. We pull your friend graph so you can see your mutuals that already have Germ in the app."

Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option.

At some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®

morning.title: Chase, Visa, Mastercard confirm third-party cyberattacks that may have exposed customers' info
morning.text:
JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants.

“Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday. “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week.”

Mastercard also cited a third-party provider in an email sent to The Register following our questions about the alleged breach.

“We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses - non-payments information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” Mastercard SVP Seth Eisen said. “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.”

JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media.

“We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.

“There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank said on Thursday.

None of the three financial firms would comment on who the third-party providers are, when the breaches occurred, and what specific data was stolen. The Register will update this story as we learn more details about the intrusions.

Extortion crew n0n claimed responsibility for all three alleged hacks, posting the financial giants to its data-leak site on Monday. The group, believed to be based in Russia, emerged in September and posted 108 victims over its first month in operations. ®

morning.title: Palo Alto Networks opens wallet for open-weight training biz
morning.text:
As AI has become a thorn in the side of the security industry, Palo Alto Networks (PAN) has reached an agreement to acquire Applied Compute, an AI model training platform.

"We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, during the company's fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Wednesday. "The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks."

So in the spirit of "hair of the dog that bit me," PAN is ingesting Applied Compute to make open-weight AI more secure for corporate customers. The answer to insecurity brought on by AI is buying security with AI.

In its announcement of the tie-up, PAN declares "the future of enterprise AI is hybrid, and that a large share of enterprises will run on open-source and open-weight models tuned to their own data, cost, and control needs."

That view has been clouded a bit by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's fall from grace: Back in July, he came to the defense of open-weight models as a defense against the hegemony of purveyors of closed-weight commercial models like Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. His resignation as CEO of Nvidia has led to worries that the open-weight ecosystem has lost some lobbying power at a time when the US is wary about the uptake of models made in China.

Nonetheless, PAN clearly sees a future for open-weight models.

"Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, in a statement. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional."

The company expects the $4.5 billion all-stock transaction to add more than $1 billion to the company's Next Generation Security business by FY 2029.

Arora, on the company's earnings call, explained the pricey bet as recognition of the corporate desire to avoid vendor lock-in and to retain control of data.

"We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open-weight and open-source models," he said. "Early signs of that shift are clear, with open-weight models growing from under 5 percent of token traffic to more than 60 percent over the past year."

Beyond the sticker price, PAN is ready to up its infrastructure ante. Arora said the biz expects to build infrastructure supporting more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity, a project that will take "a modest CapEx commitment of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030." ®

morning.text: AI Claude maker Anthropic made a splash on Nasdaq on Wednesday as it debuted 34% higher than its IPO price under the symbol ANT at a time when investor concerns over heavy spending and profitability have dragged AI and related stocks lower.Anthropic stock began trading on Nasdaq at $111.50 per share, 34% higher than its IPO price of $83 allotted to early shareholders.The company's market valuation hit $2.09 trillion in the first 10 minutes of trading, surpassing the market cap of recently listed SpaceX, founded by Elon Musk.The stock pared its opening gains, but closed at $97.17, which was 17.07% higher over its IPO price.The company priced its IPO at $83 on Wednesday evening, above the initially indicated range of $70-$78, and expanded the number of shares on offer from 833 million to 980 million, taking the Claude chatbot maker’s valuation to $1.5 trillion despite concerns over the outlook for a key pillar of the AI boom.The IPO price came in significantly higher than expected, despite mounting investor concerns following the dramatic ouster of Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, a leading figure in the AI industry, amid a potential Chinese espionage scandal.Separate from the IPO, Anthropic also lined up $26 billion in private placements with major tech partners including Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia.For live updates on US Markets, click here"The ANT IPO saw strong demand, giving a near-term boost to sentiment in the AI ecosystem. Demand for computing power remains strong, so this is not an industry in imminent collapse, but there is a realignment of marginal winners and losers among investors, and those with existing computing power in a stronger position than those without. So hyperscalers, with strong balance sheets and cash flows may be better positioned than those more exposed to the pure growth of data center buildout," said Michael Rosen, CIO, Angeles Investments, according to Reuters.“It’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia,” said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co, according to AP. “The pricing shows strong demand among investors.”Strong demand for Anthropic shares, despite a broader tech selloff, highlights investors' continued appetite for pure-play AI companies even as enthusiasm for the sector has cooled in recent weeks."Anthropic maybe one of the few AI stocks that holds up in the near term, while the rest of the AI trade still faces questions," Ben Reitzes, analyst at Melius Research, told Reuters, as he started coverage on the stock with a "buy" rating and a 24-month price target of $155. Melius' target, the highest so far among analysts that have launched coverage, implies an upside of nearly 87% from Anthropic's IPO price.Also Read: Anthropic IPO leaves more than half of institutional investors empty-handedBrokerages expect the company's revenues to around $400 million by 2029. A syndicate of more than 20 banks was involved in the IPO, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley working as the lead underwriters.Anthropic’s stock market debut marks a shift in the AI investment boom, moving investor attention from companies supplying the chips and infrastructure powering advanced models to the AI developers themselves. With hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into chips and data centres, leading AI labs now face the challenge of scaling revenues fast enough to justify their massive spending commitments.The rapid pace of AI development has also sparked growing debate over safety. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is among those urging leading AI companies to “pace the frontier” and prioritise safeguards. In its IPO filing, Anthropic cautioned that AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” without adequate safety measures and regulatory oversight.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

morning.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning
morning.text:
arXiv:2611.09154v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.
